At matched time-frequency bin-removal budgets, a simple low-energy-first policy achieves higher mean wideband PESQ than random deletion and the tested psychoacoustic masking criteria. At 50% removal in the spreading-matrix comparison, energy, masking, and random policies score 4.46, 3.60, and 1.19 on Piper, and 3.42, 2.10, and 1.22 on Kokoro. Spectrograms and masking maps expose where these perturbations fall and why a model's below-threshold regions cannot automatically be treated as inaudible. Calibration diagnostics show substantial threshold sensitivity, while a small single-listener pilot establishes no transparent removal budget. CPU profiles identify waveform decoding as the main measured kernel cost, but a tested dynamic-INT8 Kokoro decoder runs slower than FP32 on both CPUs. The results establish energy ranking as a strong oracle baseline and motivate testing perceptual allocation inside a decoder. They do not yet demonstrate saved computation: the decisions here use already synthesized audio, and quality metrics are evaluated at 16 kHz. We release scripts, results, audio examples, and a listening-study instrument.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Terrain Traversal Without Motion Priors: Expert-Routed Humanoid Locomotion at Deployment Fidelity
item.description: arXiv:2610.14061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: State-of-the-art perceptive humanoid locomotion is mostly built on retargeted motion capture, a generative motion prior, and a distillation stage. We report a complete system that does not require this pipeline for a humanoid to cross varied terrain. In its place, we provide a five-expert mixture routed by a terrain classifier over a sensed elevation grid, and target every foothold with a model-based planner, refined by six closed-form-gradient steps on an interpolated terrain-cost field instead of picked from a fixed grid. Driven through the same perception-to-actuation software a robot would run, inside a second, deployment-fidelity simulator, it crosses an $85$\,m five-segment waypoint course $18$ of $20$ times end-to-end ($90\%$, Wilson $95\%$ CI $70$--$97$) and succeeds $20/20$ on four of five segments scored alone, where an ablated configuration without the mixture and without refinement reaches $0\%$ on both the stair and the hurdle segment. The continuous refinement moves $72.4\%$ of foot placements across at least one grid-cell boundary, which produces real sub-grid correction. We also ran matched component studies to report what does not account for it: one expert equals five on the training distribution, four label-free routers collapse to near-uniform activation, and a self-supervised terrain embedding loses to the privileged label.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Grover Search for a Threshold-Fraction Variant of the Travelling Salesman Problem: A Circuit-Level Construction
item.description: arXiv:2610.14062v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Travelling Salesman Problem (TSP) is a classic combinatorial optimisation problem which is NP-hard in optimisation form and NP-complete as a decision problem. The standard question asks for the shortest tour that visits every city exactly once and returns to the origin. This paper studies a threshold-fraction variant, which we call the robust TSP, formulated as a promise problem: given a distance threshold $K$ and a promised fraction $p$, decide whether at least a fraction $p$ of all tours have total length at most $K$, or whether no such tour exists. We show that Grover's quantum search algorithm decides this problem using $O(1/\sqrt{p})$ oracle queries, independent of the number of cities $N$, with each query implemented by a quantum circuit of polynomial size in $N$. For any fixed robustness level $p$, the total runtime is therefore polynomial in $N$. Measured in oracle queries, the quantum algorithm offers a quadratic improvement in the dependence on $1/p$ over classical random sampling, which needs $\Theta(1/p)$ samples; because each quantum query is costly, however, it is faster in total running time only when $p$ is very small (roughly below $N^{-4}$), where the number of queries is no longer constant. We describe the problem formulation, detail the oracle construction (edge-length loading, sequential quantum addition, and threshold comparison), and analyse the query complexity to achieve the required result.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Auditing LLM Program Search for Bermudan Stopping with Primal--Dual Certificates
item.description: arXiv:2610.14063v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM program-search agents are usually judged by the score that drives their search. We study LLM-driven search over Python exercise policies for Bermudan options, an optimal stopping problem where a trusted evaluator owns the simulation and a dual upper bound~$U$. For any policy, $0 \le V^\star - L_\pi \le U - L_\pi$; we report Monte Carlo estimates of both bounds with their sampling error. We audit 24 generation attempts from two pipelines, a six-pair feedback-representation ablation, and a holdout evaluated after selection was frozen. No selected generated program improves on Ridge LSMC consistently or by more than Monte Carlo uncertainty; holdout gap scores lie within $0.002$ of it. On six one-dimensional puts, a high-precision binomial reference places Ridge within Monte Carlo noise of optimal and attributes 99\% of the estimated gap to dual-bound looseness, so this dual audits validity but cannot certify progress at the search's scale. Structured memory showed no benefit over score-only memory in this ablation. Whether search ``worked'' depends on reporting rules: retaining the initial reference, freezing selection before holdout, and counting failures.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Do My Samples Help? Compute Budget Allocation for Real-World Sampling-Based MPC in Contact-Rich Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sampling-based model predictive control (SMPC) is increasingly practical for contact-rich manipulation because GPU-based physics simulators enable real-time evaluation of large numbers of non-differentiable contact rollouts. However, this computation budget is finite and can be spent in competing ways, including denser control exploration, representing dynamics or state uncertainty, replanning more frequently, or aligning the simulation better with the physical state. Yet, the resulting trade-offs are not well understood in real-world sim-to-real control. In this work, we address this question through a systematic study of how to allocate a fixed computation budget for SMPC in contact-rich manipulation. To enable controlled comparisons, we develop a GPU-based framework named Budget-Allocating Model Predictive Control (BAMPC), which runs on MuJoCo Warp and exposes dynamics uncertainty, state uncertainty, and temporal alignment as independent dimensions of the computation budget while using the same control stack in simulation and on a real robot. Across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, we find that the best budget allocation depends on the dominant sim-to-real error, with dynamics randomization not universally the most effective one.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Safety-Oriented Trajectory Ranking from BEV Perception Outputs
item.description: arXiv:2610.14066v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bird's-Eye-View (BEV) representations are increasingly used as compact inputs for autonomous driving perception and planning. However, lightweight and interpretable methods for evaluating candidate ego trajectories directly on BEV outputs remain useful for vehicular safety workflows, rapid prototyping, and human-in-the-loop validation. This paper presents a modular trajectory ranking pipeline that consumes BEVFusion object detections and map segmentations derived from nuScenes sensor data and ranks manually specified candidate trajectories according to safety-first criteria. The ranking prioritizes avoiding collisions and walkway violations, then smaller end distance to the target, and finally path efficiency. To study whether these rule-based rankings resemble human judgment, we created seven BEV traffic scenarios and compared the script output with preferences from a survey of 21 participants. Across 146 pairwise votes, 124 matched the trajectory ranked first by the evaluator, corresponding to an overall agreement of 84.9 %. The results indicate that simple BEV-centric safety heuristics can approximate human preferences in constrained trajectory choice tasks while remaining transparent enough for analysis, dataset curation, and autonomous driving studies.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] From Hitter to Player: Separating Motor Execution and Strategy in Competitive Humanoid Table Tennis
item.description: arXiv:2610.14067v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Competitive humanoid table tennis requires two distinct abilities: executing a desired return and deciding where to return the ball. We separate these two problems, with the ball landing target serving as an interface between motor control and strategy. (1) We first train a whole-body motor policy conditioned on the desired landing target, which maps the target to an executable humanoid stroke through a model-based strike planner and a learned controller. (2) We then improve the motor policy through self-play in closed-loop rallies, where the robot learns to handle incoming balls generated by another player rather than only prescribed incoming balls. At this stage, the landing targets are still sampled without considering the opponent, so the policy improves its execution without learning game strategy. (3) Finally, we freeze the entire motor stack and train a stroke-level strategic policy to choose landing targets through competitive self-play. Motor self-play improves both landing accuracy and legal-return rate during rallies. More importantly, with the entire motor stack fixed, changing only the target-selection policy leads to large differences in game outcomes: the learned strategy wins 89%, 82%, and 73% of points against center, random, and away-from-opponent baselines, respectively. The learned strategy also changes where it sends the ball according to the opponent's position and the previous target, showing that self-play learns more than simply aiming at fixed "good" locations. On hardware, the same frozen execution stack and strategic interface support complete 11-point games against a recreational human opponent, including multi-stroke rallies with both forehand and backhand returns.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Loose Lips: Understanding Privacy Leakage in Agentic Dialogue
item.description: arXiv:2610.14071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLM agents are increasingly deployed in high-stakes enterprise settings, understanding how they handle sensitive information in agentic dialogue has become critical. Privacy leakage in such settings requires reasoning about whether information flows respect the contextual norms under which they originated. We extend CIMemories to CIMEMORIES DIALOGUE, a benchmark of 4,410 two-agent dialogue instances grounded in Contextual Integrity theory. Using this benchmark, we systematically evaluate 7 open-weight models from the Qwen3 and Llama 3.1 families across conversation lengths of 1 and 6 turns under three prompting conditions. We find that task capability and privacy leakage are fundamentally coupled: more capable models are systematically leakier, with no model in our evaluation able to decouple the two. Thinking models consistently leak more than their non-thinking counterparts, a pattern we attribute to the extended reasoning surface created by chain-of-thought. Leakage compounds with conversation length, rising up to 3x from 1 to 6 turns. Our results suggest that the coupling between task capability and privacy leakage is not an artifact of misconfiguration but a structural feature of current agentic systems.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Is the Future Predictable? Modeling Future Predictability for Reliable Temporal Reasoning
item.description: arXiv:2610.14073v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) remain unreliable when reasoning about the future. Existing models often overlook the difference among future states, committing to specific answers even when the queried facts are inherently volatile. To capture this challenge, we introduce ChronoRegime, a future-oriented temporal reasoning task that requires models to determine whether historical temporal evidence justifies commitment to a future answer. Furthermore, we propose Confidence-Aware Temporal Reasoning (CTR), a framework that estimates future predictability from temporal dynamics and regulates answer commitment accordingly. Rather than performing unconditional forecasting, CTR commits only when the reconstructed evidence supports the target future state. Across multiple LLMs, CTR improves strict overall accuracy by 6.7 percentage points and reduces hallucination rates by 18.4 percentage points on average over the plain QA baseline. These results demonstrate that explicit predictability assessment is an effective mechanism for safer and more reliable temporal reasoning under future uncertainty.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] One Model, Multiple Compute Budgets: Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE for Flexible Compute Across Turns
item.description: arXiv:2610.14074v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models typically support different inference budgets through separate model sizes or fixed compute configurations. In multi-turn interactions, however, compute demand can vary substantially across turns. Using a high-compute model for every turn wastes computation, while routing among independent models may require rebuilding model-specific history states after switches. We therefore ask whether a single shared model can support multiple compute budgets that can be flexibly assigned across turns. We introduce Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE, which jointly supports token-to-concept compression ratios of 2, 4, and 8 (CR2/CR4/CR8) within a shared backbone. Lightweight full-token modules reduce compression-independent cost, ratio-specific boundary routers support distinct compression levels, and cross-ratio training enables mixed-ratio processing within the same context. Across PTBench and SFTBench, the three fixed modes outperform their compute-matched MoE baselines in all 6 comparisons while remaining competitive with independently trained fixed-ratio specialists. On CodeChat and CoSQL, mixed-ratio inference improves the accuracy--compute trade-off, outperforming the Large MoE by 5.87 and 2.68 percentage points while reducing FLOPs by 41.1% and 12.3%, respectively. Under the same turn-wise budget schedule, Multi-Ratio ConceptMoE further reduces FLOPs by 78.4% and 46.9% relative to routing among independent models. These results demonstrate that a single shared model can provide multiple compute budgets for flexible compute allocation across turns.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Assessing the Marginal Utility of Exocentric Head Views in UMI-Style Large-FoV Wrist-Camera Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-view perception is often treated as a safe design choice for robot manipulation: if one camera is useful, more cameras should be better. We revisit that assumption in tabletop bimanual manipulation by comparing policies trained with two large-field-of-view (FoV) wrist cameras against policies that additionally receive a head view, using controlled-variable experiments on a real bimanual platform. Across three tabletop tasks, adding a head view does not consistently improve task completion or execution quality: when the wrist cameras already observe the objects, grippers, and goal regions, wrist-only policies form a strong baseline. Restricting the wrist-camera FoV increases the potential value of a head view, but performance improves most reliably when the added view supplies concentrated, task-relevant information: region-of-interest (ROI) cropping yields more consistent head-view gains than the uncropped image, which is dominated by background and task-irrelevant regions. The data-scaling results further suggest an interaction between FoV and demonstration count: wide observations improve coverage but may require more data to stabilize, and they may reach a higher performance ceiling once enough demonstrations are available. These results suggest that camera design should be framed as a task-relevance and information-density problem rather than as a simple count of input views.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Two-Stage Multi-modal Learning for Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation: From Physical Alignment to Scene Aggregation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14077v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embodied Audio-Visual Navigation (AVN) requires an agent to locate sound targets by jointly leveraging visual and auditory cues. While prior work has achieved notable success with static sound sources, real-world scenarios often involve moving targets, giving rise to the more challenging problem of \textbf{Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation (D-AVN)}. Existing approaches largely rely on semantic auditory features, which limits generalization to unheard sound categories and hinders fine-grained spatial reasoning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel \textbf{Two-Stage Multi-modal Learning} framework for D-AVN. In the Physical Alignment stage, the proposed \textbf{Intensity-Calibrated Geometry Encoder (ICGE)} performs physics-informed alignment of sound intensity with visual geometry to capture category-agnostic spatial correspondence. In the Scene Aggregation stage, a Transformer-based \textbf{Cross-Modal Scene Aggregator (CMSA)} dynamically integrates multi-modal features to construct a robust state representation for policy learning. Extensive experiments on Replica and Matterport3D demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art success rates, while significantly improving generalization and navigation efficiency in complex environments and under unheard sound scenarios.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] SenseWeather: Multimodal Sensing for Robust Robotic Perception under Extreme Conditions
item.description: arXiv:2610.14082v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Robotic perception must remain reliable when extreme environmental conditions severely degrade the primary RGB observation. Although robotic platforms commonly carry complementary sensors such as depth and infrared, much of the modern perception stack remains RGB-centric, creating a mismatch between multimodal onboard sensing and pretrained downstream models. We study whether complementary sensing can be used upstream to recover a task-compatible RGB observation that preserves existing perception capabilities without modifying or retraining the downstream stack. To this end, we introduce SenseWeather, a controlled multimodal benchmark for robotic perception under severe rain, snow, dust, fog, and darkness, with registered RGB, depth, and infrared observations, clean references, and grounded high-level perception tasks. We further develop Fusion-to-RGB, with two parameter-efficient sensor-fusion realizations based on token-space fusion for a diffusion transformer and residual latent conditioning for an inpainting UNet. Across frozen open-vocabulary grounding and vision-language models, RGB+D+IR fusion improves all paired downstream comparisons over the corresponding RGB-only restorers, including AP50 gains across all ten detector comparisons. Importantly, these perception gains do not consistently follow conventional image-fidelity metrics, and increasing weather severity does not induce monotonic downstream degradation. These results show that complementary sensing can preserve reusable robotic perception under extreme conditions, while highlighting task-level perception robustness as an objective distinct from visual restoration quality.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] SAGE: Efficient Protected Vision-Language Inference on Smart Glasses
item.description: arXiv:2610.14089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Smart glasses are a promising platform for vision-language assistants, but private split inference remains expensive: protecting visual representations before transmission does not remove the cost of on-device vision encoding, wide protected tokens, or hardware-unaware execution. We present SAGE (Smart-glasses-Aware Guarded Encoding), a hardware-aware framework for efficient protected VLM inference on smart glasses. SAGE keeps raw images and unprotected visual tokens on the trusted device, reduces visual input cost, executes shape-specialized INT8 graphs, and compresses protected representations into compact 256-dimensional INT8 packets before transmission. Unlike efficiency methods optimized only for nominal model size, SAGE selects its operating point using downstream answer quality together with measured latency, memory, and thermal behavior on real Mentra Live glasses. On a matched Qwen workload, SAGE reduces glasses inference latency by 39.18%, device-sensor temperature rise by 21.91%, and protected packet size by 96.56%, while retaining 85.62% of the protected reference's relaxed utility and comparable prompted containment. Direct glasses-to-phone tests deliver all 192 packets and reduce median packet-plus-acknowledgment time from 71.3 to 10.0 ms. The compact protected interface also transfers across four additional VLM families. These results show that private wearable VLM inference must be optimized jointly across representation protection, communication, and real-device execution rather than through model compression alone.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] When pose graphs are not enough: a failure analysis of pose-graph-based camera estimation for Gaussian splatting
item.description: arXiv:2610.14090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exterior Gaussian-splat twins for real-estate listings are captured to a fixed recipe: a consumer drone orbits a single property in several overlapping passes at stepped altitudes, with occasional vertical ascents, so the imagery is dense, sequential, GPS- and time-tagged, and revisits each facade from many angles. This structure is tantalizing: it suggests camera poses could be recovered by a dense pose-graph optimization (PGO) whose only unknowns are the poses, far fewer than the joint pose-and-point problem bundle adjustment (BA) solves. PGO is mature in robotics, but almost always as post-processing: it redistributes the drift of an already-decent trajectory once loop closures tie it together. Splatting captures push that regime to its limit, every frame closing loops with dozens of others, raising a clean question: does pose-only optimization reach BA accuracy? We built a system specialized to this capture structure, not a general-purpose SfM tool, to test it. It beat COLMAP on speed but never on quality; this paper is the candid post-mortem. The shortfall arises from several interacting causes, hand-set weights, greedy merging and a noisy GPS ruler, together with two limits inherent to the formulation: SE(3) edges carry no scale degree of freedom, so independently scaled sub-maps drift when merged, and a two-view edge stops short of the coupling one 3D point imposes on every frame that sees it. A viable design must add back Sim(3) constraints, absolute GPS priors, retained structure, and uncertainty-aware weighting
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Pristine Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.14091v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Training on broad, unfiltered data enables high-quality image generation, but can also teach models concepts that should not be generated; restricting the training data ensures safety, but reduces quality because examples containing unsafe concepts also provide useful knowledge that is not itself unsafe. Existing approaches largely address this trade-off post hoc through concept unlearning, which can lead to catastrophic forgetting as the number of concepts to remove grows. We instead ask whether unsafe concept knowledge can be compartmentalized during pretraining so that access to it can be disabled at inference. We introduce Pristine Models, a novel text-to-image generation architecture with an attention mechanism that encourages the separation of safe and unsafe knowledge into independently parameterized branches. The branch-specific parameters are learned during training, while the unsafe branch can be detached at inference. On ImageNet, Pristine Models enable safer generation while retaining much of the utility of full-data pretraining, achieving higher image quality and better text alignment than training only on safe data or applying post-hoc concept removal. We further scale our approach to CC12M, demonstrating that it remains effective in a substantially larger and more diverse open-world pretraining setting.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Lava: Foundations for Liquid Haskell via Translation to Rocq
item.description: arXiv:2610.14092v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Liquid Haskell is an extension of the Glasgow Haskell compiler (GHC) that adds support for refinement types: types restricted by logical predicates. Specifications are automatically checked by an SMT solver, thus offering lightweight verification directly within the language. However, the necessarily large trusted codebase behind Liquid Haskell (from GHC to the SMT solver to the refinement typechecker itself) raises the question of trust in the verification and the necessity for a formalized semantics of Liquid Haskell linked to its implementation. Grounding Liquid Haskell in theory is complicated by the interaction between two semantic levels in the language: a computational one and a logical one (for refinement predicates). While both are well understood separately, their interaction is subtle and has only been partially described. We give a semantics to Liquid Haskell by translation to Rocq. Both the computational and logical parts are translated to the same language, with a well-understood semantics; our translation makes the discrepancy between the two semantic levels explicit. The translation is implemented in Haskell and comes with a Rocq library that includes powerful proof automation standing in for the SMT solver. Thus, on the practical level, our tool Lava serves as a certificate checker for the supported subset of Liquid Haskell.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Human Pose Estimation by Probabilistic Mixtures of Gaussian and Uniform Distributions
item.description: arXiv:2610.14093v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite advancements in sub-pixel decoding, modern Human Pose Estimation (HPE) architectures remain constrained by deterministic coordinate extraction from discrete heatmaps, which systematically fails under dense occlusions and Out-of-Distribution (OoD) ambiguities. To address these limitations, we propose a post-hoc continuous probabilistic framework that intercepts raw heatmaps and models them as a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) augmented with a spatially agnostic uniform distribution, requiring no architectural modifications or retraining. This continuous representation allows us to comprehensively explore the distinct contributions of density modeling to HPE. We show that the spatial expectation of our fitted GMM achieves precision parity with leading sub-pixel decoders without heuristic post-processing. Leveraging this continuous space, our test-time augmentation aggregates probability distributions rather than discrete activations, mitigating multi-scale heatmap poisoning. Furthermore, because our multimodal GMM parameterization isolates competing spatial hypotheses, it naturally interfaces with geometric regularizers such as Markov Random Fields. However, our analysis exposes the inherent vulnerabilities of 2D kinematic priors under perspective foreshortening and visual degradation. Crucially, this density formulation yields significant improvements in uncertainty quantification: our calibrated geometric covariance volume outperforms standard peak-intensity heuristics in OoD anomaly detection under severe occlusion. For in-distribution calibration, dynamically fusing our geometric metric via Adaptive Softmax reduces or matches baseline Area Under the Sparsification Error (AUSE) across benchmarks and degradation levels. Finally, we establish that this continuous parameterization is extensible to multi-view 3D architectures, bypassing the $\mathcal{O}(N^3)$ voxel memory bottleneck.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Scenes as an Attack Surface: Uncovering Scene-Grounded Safety Failures in MLLMs
item.description: arXiv:2610.14094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing jailbreak attacks have exposed serious safety weaknesses in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Most prior attacks rely on specially constructed visual inputs to carry or support harmful intent. In this paper, we uncover a different vulnerability: task-relevant scene semantics alone can shift an MLLM from refusal to compliance, even when the visual input introduces no additional attack instructions and the original task intent remains unchanged. We formalize this failure as a scene-grounded visual safety vulnerability and introduce SceneSafetyBench to investigate it across eight risk categories and nine white- and black-box MLLMs. Our analysis reveals that this failure is associated with how task-relevant visual evidence influences downstream safety representations, suggesting that visual grounding alone cannot fully explain the observed safety shift. Building on this finding, we propose Scene-Grounded Attacks (SGA), which preserve the original task while constructing validated scene-grounded queries and combining their independent responses. Across nine target MLLMs, SGA achieves an average attack success rate (ASR) of 86.17%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 8.55 percentage points and achieving the highest ASR on eight models. Our results identify scene semantics as an overlooked attack surface in MLLMs and highlight a growing tension between stronger visual grounding and robust multimodal safety alignment.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] SWEeper-Bench: Can Agents Discover Bugs in Interactive Software?
item.description: arXiv:2610.14096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents increasingly interact with users by generating interactive software on the fly rather than replying in text, yet many bugs in such software reveal themselves only after multi-step interactions. Today, users must discover these bugs and wait for fixes, making the development loop slow and expensive. Existing benchmarks typically assume the bugs have already been identified, leaving agents' ability to find interaction-dependent failures largely unevaluated. We introduce SWEeper-Bench, 200 tasks built from real bug fixes in 200 widely used open-source web applications. Each task gives the agent only the codebase and an open-ended request such as "Find and fix issues in Focalboard's board sharing and membership." Because these bugs are hard to detect from code alone, agents must design interactive tests to uncover them. An agentic verifier then judges each repair by what a user would observe in the browser. The best of 15 frontier agents passes only 59.0% of tasks. Through stage-by-stage analysis of agent trajectories, we show that the biggest bottleneck is identifying the buggy behavior: agents often reach the relevant feature but never trigger the failure or fail to recognize it. SWEeper-Bench measures progress toward agents that close this loop themselves, delivering software that works without waiting for user feedback.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] A Physics-Informed Hybrid Forward-Inverse Machine Learning Framework for High-Dimensional Sparse Recipe Reconstruction
item.description: arXiv:2610.14097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-dimensional sparse recipe formulation in process industries involves nonlinear association of various covariates, bounded by sparsity constraints and multi-criteria tolerances. Traditional physics-based classical methods (such as Kubelka-Munk) fail to generate sparse candidate recipes properly due to their simplified assumptions and industrial process variations. This study proposes a hybrid physics-informed uncertainty-aware framework that is structured into three modules: (a) Module A, a multi-target forward quality model; (b) Module B, a sparse inverse reconstructor; and (c) Module C, a feasibility-constrained ranking layer. Then it has been validated in an industrial textile dyeing context with recipe-grouped cross-validation under multi-illuminant quality assessment comprising process and production information, target reflectance, K/S values, and spectral descriptors. Histogram Gradient Boosting (HGB) with spectral-only features ($R_\lambda$, K/S) and Gradient Boosting Regressor (GBDT) with recipe-process features outperforms other configurations with out-of-Fold MAE of 0.1655 and 0.1523 in the forward quality model. For inverse reconstruction, a component-wise median blend achieved a recipe-vector MAE of 0.0295. Exploratory conditional treatment effect (CATE) suggests an observational association that alkali adjustment reduces error for red and pale shades (CATE = -0.196). This framework provides a human-in-the-loop decision-support tool that minimizes costly laboratory trials across industrial formulation domains.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] From Prototype to Massing: Learning Graph Correspondence for Scalable Facade Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2610.14098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Facade articulation at building scale is usually resolved manually or through parametric systems that encode design intent as explicit rules. This paper investigates a complementary workflow in which a designer-authored prototype supplies transferable articulation logic. Prototype and target massing are represented as heterogeneous attributed graphs, and a Siamese graph attention network with instance-local triplet supervision embeds their segments in a shared metric space. Many-to-one nearest-neighbor retrieval then routes prototype Patterns to the larger target. On the original 85/15 within-corpus holdout, prototype-to-massing top-1 accuracy reached 96.5%, compared with a reported 76.5% raw-feature baseline. A Rhino demonstrator converts predicted correspondence into reusable facade Patterns, and qualitative applications on four built projects show the workflow across distinct massing organizations. The contribution is not automated facade generation, but an authoring model in which resolved geometry serves as a computational specification for project-scale propagation.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Fin_Agent at FinEval 2026: Task-Aware Methods for Multilingual Financial NLP
item.description: arXiv:2610.14101v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Fin_Agent, our submission to the FinEval 2026 shared task on multilingual fi nancial language understanding. Our sys tems address Greek financial named-entity recognition, Japanese implicit communication recognition, and multilingual financial ques tion answering. For Greek NER, we com bine annotation-aware numeric rules with zero shot Qwen2.5-32B classification, achieving 0.9521 public F1 and 0.8884 private F1. For Japanese implicit communication, an inter pretable cue-based ordinal scorer achieves 98.0% test accuracy. For multilingual financial QA, BGE-M3retrieval with Qwen3-32B gen eration achieves 0.3023 and 0.3419 ROUGE-1 F1 on the public and private splits. Key limita tions include dataset-specific rules, handcrafted cues, and limited supervision. Implementa tion code is available https://github.com/ Rashidnira/finagent-fineval-2026.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Embodied Zero-Shot Task Planning via Hardware-Aware LLM-VLM Integration for Grounded Robotic Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14106v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models can translate natural-language instructions into plausible manipulation plans, but robotic execution requires physically grounded decisions that respect robot embodiment, workspace geometry, reachability, collision constraints, and grasp feasibility. This paper presents a hardware-aware large language model-vision-language model (LLM-VLM) manipulation framework for a simulated Franka Research 3 robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The framework separates symbolic reasoning from metric execution: an API-hosted LLM planner receives a structured scene summary and generates only symbolic task information, including the object to manipulate, target relation, approach preference, and objects to avoid. A local Qwen3-VL 8B VLM verifier supports semantic confirmation of ambiguous objects and open-container surrogates. Both the LLM planner and the VLM verifier are prohibited from generating robot coordinates, grasp poses, keepout dimensions, gripper commands, trajectory waypoints, or success labels. Instead, these decisions are handled by deterministic grounding and execution modules that use the robot model, scene geometry, MoveIt 2 collision checking, inverse kinematics, grasp validation, release verification, and final visual assessment. Execution feedback is returned only as symbolic context for replanning. The framework is evaluated through simulated digital-twin trials involving pickup, occluded-source access, keepout reasoning, relation placement, and sequential manipulation tasks.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] The weight enumerators of irreducible cyclic codes of length $2^\ell$
item.description: arXiv:2610.14107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Using the spectral relation between irreducible cyclic codes (ICC) and generalized Paley (GP) graphs recently found by the authors, we study the weight distribution of irreducible cyclic codes of length $2^\ell$, $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$. These codes were previously studied by Sharma, Bakshi and Raka, who divided them into two families (each having two cases). First we characterize the GP-graphs spectrally related to these families of ICCs: they are complete, semiprimitive, Hamming, or Cartesian products of semiprimitive GP-graphs. We then compute the spectrum of these graphs and hence, by the mentioned spectral relation we finally obtain neat explicit expressions for the weight enumerators of all the irreducible cyclic codes of length $2^\ell$ with $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Does System One Transfer? Calibrated Typed-Decision Models, Label Budgets, and Translation for Indonesian Regional Languages
item.description: arXiv:2610.14112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Calibrated typed-decision ("System One") models return a label and a probability in a single forward pass at a small fraction of the cost of large language models (LLMs), yet their evaluation has been almost entirely English. We report a pre-registered evaluation of the commercial Jev model and the open Laya-multilingual model on Indonesian regional languages, using the parallel NusaX sentiment (12 languages) and NusaTranslation sentiment and emotion (7 languages) test sets. Jev is more often correct on sentences that are lexically closer to Indonesian in all three datasets, and presenting the human Indonesian translation instead raises its accuracy by up to 37.2 points, most in languages distant from Indonesian. Its expected calibration error does not grow on regional languages, but its ability to rank its own errors degrades in all three datasets. Retrained classifiers need more than 500 labels per language to match zero-shot Jev in 9 of 10 NusaX regional languages. A confidence-gated cascade that sends Jev's 10-30% least confident decisions to a local IndoBERT classifier matches or exceeds the better of the two systems, and routing to an LLM instead matches that LLM at 24-77% lower API cost. Of six further commercial LLMs (three Claude and three GPT models), five are 4-14 points more accurate than Jev, at several hundred times the API cost where it is reported, while the smallest (Claude Haiku) is less accurate. We release the pre-registration, code and all predictions.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] MeshRepair: Autoregressive Topology Repair for Generated Artisan Meshes
item.description: arXiv:2610.14113v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent artisan mesh generation methods produce meshes whose topology comes close to the preferences of human artists. But gaps to artist quality remain because generated meshes commonly contain holes, stray faces, and duplicated faces. Regenerating a mesh from scratch is costly, and a new draw may change the preferred topology entirely or introduce errors elsewhere. In this work we study artisan topology correction. The task is to correct the topology of a generated mesh (the draft) in place, toward the layout an artist would make. We propose a method for this task. It is a face-level correction network based on a prefix-LM. It reads the mesh bidirectionally and emits an edit sequence autoregressively. The sequence consists of a deletion phase followed by an addition phase. We propose the novel formulation of the deletion head which picks faces to delete autoregressively and the addition head that selects vertices to form a face to add. The addition head also adds vertices when needed. Untouched faces pass through unchanged, so the corrected mesh keeps the vertices and the layout of the draft. The draft enters as a prefix and only the edits are generated. A correction therefore takes far fewer decoding steps than generating every face again with an autoregressive mesh generator. We benchmark our method against repair tools on scripted defects and on held-out drafts from two mesh generators. Across both scripted defects and generated drafts, our method improves the quad-equivalent face F1, removes non-manifold faces, and cleans up the topology.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] The Silent Failures in Agentic Data Science
item.description: arXiv:2610.14115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models have significantly lowered the barrier to writing code. Naturally, this has also led to the development of data science agents that promise automating the design and execution of data science from task formulation to model development. Existing evaluations of agentic data science (agentic DS) assess downstream predictive performance and code correctness, providing preliminary insight in agentic DS capabilities. We argue that these evaluations overlook the fundamental principles of data science: methodological data science- and domain knowledge. As such, only assessing downstream performance masks methodological failures such as data leakage and inappropriate validation, limiting the development of robust agentic DS systems. In this paper, we evaluate agentic DS beyond accuracy from three different angles: 1) a large-scale analysis of failure modes in common agentic DS frameworks and models across 220 data science tasks, 2) a reusable and extensible test suite with curated data science tasks that test for six specific failures in a controlled manner, and 3) a qualitative assessment of agentic DS pipelines against expert solutions on Kaggle competitions. We find that the majority of agentic solutions contain at least one failure mode despite the complexity of agentic harness or model capacity. Moreover, we identify a positive correlation between the occurrence of data leakage failures and predictive performance, confirming the necessity to evaluate agents beyond accuracy. Our qualitative analysis shows that DS agents generally lack problem solving creativity and domain knowledge, compared to competition-winning data scientists. We believe that principled failure mode analysis, as presented here, should be integral part of agentic DS evaluations, and that the insights we surface will be key in developing trustworthy agentic DS pipelines.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] An Empirical Case Study of Prompt Engineering Strategies for Bypassing Multi-Layer Agent Security Defenses
item.description: arXiv:2610.14116v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The OpenClaw Security Attack and Defense Challenge evaluates AI agent robustness through a three-stage defense pipeline: skill file scanning (Stage 1), instruction safety evaluation (Stage 2), and attack trajectory scoring (Stage 3). This paper presents an empirical case study of prompt engineering strategies against these layers across 19 attack targets in Enterprise OA, E-commerce, and Smart Home scenarios. I document both successful and failed strategies, with an emphasis on the observed trade-off between instruction safety (Stage 2) and attack execution accuracy (Stage 3). The final online score is 0.2630, with 5 of 19 tasks achieving full bypass. The results suggest that multi-layer defenses, reinforced by built-in behavioral constraints, substantially limit what prompt engineering alone can achieve.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Make {\pi}0.5 Learn to Call Astra for Reliable Robot Manipulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14117v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GPT-6 Astra provides robust embodied reasoning, but frequent external queries increase inference time and token costs. We equip a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ policy with a lightweight CALL head that learns to predict when assistance is necessary. CALL reuses features from the standard policy forward pass and operates locally without consulting external models. Astra is activated solely for critical recovery events and returns control to $\pi_{0.5}$ upon stabilization. Evaluated across 40 LIBERO tasks (200 episodes), our system achieves a 97.5% success rate, outperforming the 95.5% baseline of pure $\pi_{0.5}$. In the Object, Goal, and Spatial suites, Astra executes only 5.49% of environment steps, consuming approximately 5,027 tokens per test episode. This selective intervention preserves the fast ordinary execution of $\pi_{0.5}$ while seamlessly integrating Astra's reasoning on demand. Our project page is available at https://kykgeek.github.io/Pi05_CALL_Astra/.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] ClawLoop: Self-Improving Agents via Harness-Native Training Loop
item.description: arXiv:2610.14118v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven their deployment toward general-purpose harness environments, where LLM-based agents operate in sandbox workspaces and interact directly with file systems and shells. While numerous post-training pipelines exist for tool-use agents, their counterparts for harness-based agents remain scarce and are predominantly one-shot and teacher-dependent: a stronger external model synthesizes tasks and collects trajectories, the target agent is trained once, and evaluation results are consumed by human researchers rather than fed back into the loop. Such pipelines are inherently bounded by the capability of the external model and the scope of human prior, leaving no room for self-improvement. To address these limitations, we propose ClawLoop, a framework that enables self-improving without any external teacher model and with minimal prior dependencies. ClawLoop composes three phases into a self-sustaining cycle: Task Synthesis, which generates a diverse pool of training tasks via two complementary construction routines, applies diagnosis-conditioned difficulty growth followed by both agent-free and agent-based task validation; Training, which updates the agent via SFT and/or RL; and Diagnosis and Feedback, which analyzes the agent's rollout behaviors to produce a capability analysis report that will be used as feedback for task synthesis in the next iteration. Using Qwen3.6-27B as the loop model, ClawLoop yields consistent improvements on SkillsBench, Claw-Eval-Live, and ClawGym-Bench. The iteratively refined tasks are further transferred to smaller-scale Qwen3.5-4B and 9B models with gains across all benchmarks, validating data quality independently of the loop model.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] The AI's Poker Face: Contrasting Persuasion and Sycophancy in Voice-Based Multi-Turn Conversations
item.description: arXiv:2610.14124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As interactions with large language models (LLMs) become increasingly routine, concerns about their capacity to influence users' beliefs grow. Yet how such influence unfolds in sustained dialogue remains insufficiently understood. We conduct a randomized controlled experiment (N=616) where participants engage in multi-turn, spoken dialogue with an LLM under three conditions: non-directive, and two directive conditions maintaining opposing stances on a polarizing topic (the merits of feminism). We examine opinion change, rhetorical strategies, and sycophancy, distinguishing the semantic content of LLM argumentation from the pragmatic strategies used to manage the interaction. Both directive conditions shifted opinions toward their assigned stances, but asymmetrically: shifts were larger for pro-feminist positions, which also elicited distinct rhetorical strategies. The non-directive condition, likewise shifted opinions pro-feminism. Social sycophancy, though near-universal, was not associated with opinion change; instead it shaped users' subjective experience. Our findings highlight distinct roles for argumentation and sycophantic accommodation in AI influence.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Quantum Annealing for Resource Allocation in Next-Generation Wireless Communication Networks: A QUBO Modeling Guide
item.description: arXiv:2610.14126v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum annealing (QA) offers a physics-inspired approach for such subproblems by mapping them onto an Ising Hamiltonian, which is algebraically equivalent to a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model executable on quantum annealers or hybrid solvers. However, their practical employment in wireless systems critically depends on the specific problem formulation, on the particular variable encoding, constraint handling, solver selection, hardware embedding, and fair benchmarking. This paper develops wireless-oriented QUBO modeling guidelines for QA-assisted resource allocation. We first present a beginner-friendly toy example in which a terrestrial-aerial resource-allocation problem with a fractional signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) maximization objective is reformulated into a two-bit QUBO via Boolean interpolation, converted into an Ising representation, and decoded back into a wireless scheduling decision. The same scheduling is applicable to UAV, aircraft, satellite, and terrestrial links in SAGIN systems. We then review the QA foundations and solver ecosystems, including binary quadratic, discrete quadratic, constrained quadratic, and hybrid models from the perspective of NG wireless optimization. Furthermore, we discuss both binary and discrete encoding, penalty-based constraint conversion, embedding overhead, solution decoding, and feasibility verification. A QUBO Compatibility Index is introduced as a lightweight diagnostic metric for assessing the associated QUBO formulation readiness, rather than a predictor of runtime or solution quality. Finally, a case study on max-min uplink power control in cell-free massive MIMO illustrates how a fairness-oriented wireless problem can be discretized, constrained, converted into the concept of a QUBO, and evaluated against classical baselines. A host of key challenges and future directions are also discussed.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Conserved amount, negotiable placement. Prompting perturbs one architecture, an AI reviewer both
item.description: arXiv:2610.14130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tesler's conservation law holds that a problem carries an irreducible amount of complexity. Brooks separates that essential part from the accidental part a solution adds. If the essential part is fixed, architecture is placement rather than quantity, and the question is which levers move placement. An AI agent implements sixty accumulating change requests on one REST endpoint under two architectures, a mutative Spring controller and an additive OfficeFloor pipeline, under five conditions, ten runs per cell, model fixed. Four are external controls, from a bare change request to the disclosed structural cost function. The fifth is different in kind. A second agent reviews each change and reasons about cohesion itself. Amount is steady. Across all ten cells the finished complexity varies by 7% to 20% over four operationalisations, and the complexity the sixty rules added by 21% to 29% within an architecture. Placement is not. Under the four external controls the plasticity ratio between the architectures is near 1 on six amount metrics (five of six intervals contain 1) against 2.7 to 10.0 on eleven placement metrics (ten of eleven above 1). The mutative architecture moves, the additive one does not, and the disclosed formula brings it to the additive arm's untouched placement. The AI reviewer is the one lever that moves the additive arm, on one family only. It consolidates the pipeline, raising change- and mass-concentration on every such metric, interval excluding zero, while leaving coupling, file count and per-node complexity untouched. The price is reported in full. Strict correctness fell in most comparisons though each rule was implemented correctly in over 99% of checkpoints, and all three outcome measures favour the concentrated codebase. The contribution is a measurable property of an architecture and its lever, not a verdict on either.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] TrustPaper for forged PDF with Issuer Fingerprints
item.description: arXiv:2610.14132v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sick leave certificates are increasingly delivered as PDF files by online teleconsultation platforms, and can be altered in minutes with free editors. Generic PDF scanners report how a file was built, but cannot tell whether that construction is legitimate: an incremental update, an embedded font or a given producer string is normal for one issuer and anomalous for another. We present TrustPaper solution, an issuer aware forensic approach that combines three elements: the claimed issuer of the document, a reference fingerprint learned beforehand from genuine documents of that issuer, and an explainable combination of evidence from several forensic modules. Fingerprints are stored as versioned declarative profiles, and every anomaly keeps its observed value, expected value and triggering rule. We formalize the threat model, the fingerprint and the scoring model, and evaluate the open-source prototype on a controlled corpus documents from two issuers and six forgery techniques. With the issuer fingerprint, all forgeries made by opportunistic and metadata-aware attackers are flagged with no false positive on genuine test documents.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Correction Training for Diffusion Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.14136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Iterative sampling in diffusion models can lead to error accumulation due to exposure bias. The denoiser is trained on real images interpolated with noise, but at inference its inputs are constructed from its own imperfect predictions from the earlier steps, something it has never seen at training time. This might be one reason diffusion models often struggle without additional help, such as CFG. We introduce a correction step for diffusion models which attempts to reduce this training-inference gap. The corrector takes the base model's prediction as input and is trained against the same ground-truth target. This makes correction an explicit learning task, with training inputs provided by the base model. During sampling, at each denoising step, we iteratively refine the denoiser's clean-sample prediction. This allows us to correct predictions at intermediate denoising steps, preventing early artifacts from persisting into the final sample. Although the corrector is trained only on predictions from the base denoiser, it can be applied repeatedly to its own outputs at inference for better results. This simple framework leads to substantial improvement in sample quality while largely preserving diversity. We evaluate our method across DiT, SiT, and JiT. Our method substantially improves upon previously reported FID scores for unguided generation and, notably, unconditional generation, where producing high-quality samples without guidance has been particularly challenging. Our method achieves performance competitive with classifier-free guidance (CFG), and combining correction with CFG further improves diversity and reduces oversaturation typical of CFG. Finally, we show that the additional inference cost of correction can be amortized by distilling the refined predictions back into the base diffusion model, retaining the quality gains without additional inference-time overhead.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] MixedTruth: Component-Level Detection of Synthetic Speech and Synthetic Background in Mixed Audio
item.description: arXiv:2610.14141v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern generative audio can fabricate not only voices but also the acoustic environments that provide evidence of when and where speech occurred. This capability undermines a longstanding forensic assumption that background sound provides reliable evidence of a recording's provenance. Yet existing detectors produce only a single real-or-synthetic verdict, leaving analysts unable to determine whether the voice, the environment, or both were manipulated. In this paper, we propose a component-level forensic detector, namely TruMix, which classifies recordings into eight categories spanning the presence and authenticity of speech and background. TruMix has a unique multi-path architecture that jointly analyzes speech-oriented and background-oriented spectral evidence, contextual information from the mixed waveform, and low-level synthesis artifacts. This design avoids the artifact propagation inherent in conventional separate-then-detect pipelines while enabling generalization across independent speech and environmental-sound generators. We also curated MixedTruth, a 4,917-hour benchmark covering all eight categories under diverse mixing conditions. Extensive experiments show that TruMix achieves 98.51% AUC for component-level attribution, significantly outperforms ten state-of-the-art synthetic-speech detectors in conventional binary classification, and exhibits strong robustness across four attack tiers.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0: Automating Diverse Task Construction and Measuring Sustained Agent Progress
item.description: arXiv:2610.14146v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon terminal benchmarks measure whether an agent can sustain progress through extended workflows with process rewards, not only whether its final state passes a binary check. We present Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench 2.0 (LHTB 2.0), an extension of Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench that preserves its 46 original tasks while correcting task and evaluation-infrastructure defects and extending 31 tasks. LHTB 2.0 contains 77 tasks across 13 domains and eight task types. The extended tasks are produced through a systematic reconstruction-task pipeline. We start from a working scientific or engineering artifact, then use a parameterized reference implementation to generate multiple scenarios, reveal six as behavioral evidence, hold out three for evaluation, and use dense progress ladders to reward partial progress while preventing memorization of public outputs. We also extend the evaluation horizon from 90 minutes to three hours and record verifier checkpoints every 30 minutes, enabling direct measurement of sustained progress within a run. Across 1,145 scored model-task runs from 15 frontier models, GPT-6-astra leads with dense mean reward 0.69 and 37 tasks at R at least 0.95, followed by GPT-5.6-sol with dense mean reward 0.67 and 32 tasks at the same threshold. On the 30 reconstruction tasks, binary verifier scores average 0.221, whereas dense ladder scores average 0.653, showing that outcome-only evaluation discards substantial intermediate progress. LHTB 2.0 provides a broader, hardened, and process-aware testbed for studying reliable agent execution over hours.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] VETNET: Assembling Benchmark Datasets for AI-Driven Veterinary Innovation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14149v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: VETNET represents an ecosystem of live benchmark datasets and evaluation frameworks designed to accelerate AI-driven innovation in animal science and veterinary medicine through standardized, high-quality datasets and multi-institutional collaboration across academic and non-academic sectors. This framework addresses the gap between AI advances in human medicine and the fragmented state of veterinary AI development.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Algorithms with Smoothed Polynomial-Time Complexity for Deterministic Discounted-sum and Mean-payoff Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.14150v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Turn-based deterministic games on graphs are two-player zero-sum games played on finite directed graphs, where the vertex set is partitioned between the Max and the adversarial Min Player. The respective player chooses outgoing edges from their vertices. We consider these games with the classical discounted-sum and mean-payoff objectives. The goal of the Max Player is to maximize the objective against the adversarial Min Player. These games lie in NP $\cap$ coNP and are among the rare combinatorial problems that belong to this complexity class, yet the existence of a polynomial-time algorithm is a major open question. All known deterministic algorithms require exponential time in the worst case, while the classical strategy iteration (policy iteration) algorithm is remarkably efficient in practice, which motivates the study of the smoothed complexity of these games. Previous results established a smoothed polynomial-time bound only for the restricted class of ergodic games and presented only a high-probability guarantee. Our main result is a new analysis technique for a variant of the strategy iteration algorithm, and we show these algorithms achieve smoothed polynomial complexity for general game graphs with both high-probability and expected runtime guarantees. In particular, our result removes the ergodicity restriction of prior work and strengthens the high-probability guarantee to the stronger expected-runtime guarantee, thereby resolving the open question on the smoothed complexity of these games.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] TrajCFG: Token-Wise Classifier-Free Guidance via Denoising Trajectory Feedback
item.description: arXiv:2610.14153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) typically applies a shared scale to all latent tokens, although their velocity predictions evolve differently during sampling. We introduce Trajectory-Adaptive Classifier-Free Guidance (TrajCFG), a training-free method for flow-matching models that adapts token-wise guidance using historical changes in guided velocity direction. TrajCFG maps this feedback to bounded scales, assigning stronger guidance to larger directional changes and weaker guidance to more consistent directions. It combines adjacent-step and interval-normalized longer-span feedback, reusing standard CFG predictions without additional model evaluations. Controlled diagnostics and ablations examine the roles of directional feedback, token-wise allocation, and history-span fusion. Experiments on text-to-video, image-to-video, text-to-audio-video, text-to-image, and image-to-3D generation show improvements over base samplers across multiple backbones. For text-to-video generation, TrajCFG improves VBench Total scores by 0.30-0.75 points over the strongest evaluated baseline on each of three backbones. These results support historical directional feedback as a broadly applicable signal for fine-grained guidance allocation. The project page is available at https://jyliu-98.github.io/trajcfg-project-page/.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Axiom-0: Hierarchical Self-Refinement for Vision-Language-Action Policies
item.description: arXiv:2610.14155v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable manipulation requires policies that generalize across tasks, layouts, and object interactions. Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine pretrained multimodal understanding with learned control, but their performance remains limited on unfamiliar task compositions. We present Axiom-0, a VLA policy that addresses both the quality of its representations and their use in action generation through hierarchical self-refinement. Intra-VLM Representation Refinement (IVRR) strengthens selected intermediate features through consistency supervision with learned feature projections during training. VLM-Action Interface Refinement (VAIR) recursively updates the resulting conditioning before action generation. Joint optimization of the supervised VLM layers, VAIR, and the action generator connects the two components. On RoboCasa365, Axiom-0 achieves 62.32% overall success in our evaluation, exceeding the highest published leaderboard score (Paimon-0, 58.1%) by 4.22 percentage points and the Xiaomi-Robotics-1 reference by 4.92 points. Under the evaluated profiling setup, mean action-chunk generation latency increases by 1.7% over Xiaomi-Robotics-1. These results demonstrate improved task completion with modest inference overhead.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] OpenMobile-2: Building Versatile Mobile Agents with Scalable Environments and App-Native Tools
item.description: arXiv:2610.14157v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce OpenMobile-2, a near-frontier mobile agent with fully open training environments and recipes. We make three key advances: (1) Diverse environments with simulated commercial apps: We build MobileGym++, featuring 35 realistic, functionally rich commercial-style apps with cross-app workflows, while preserving full controllability for reset and verification. Together with newly configured apps in Android emulators, this yields a diverse playground spanning over 110 apps. (2) Open training data at scale: Building on this foundation, we curate nearly 12K mobile interaction trajectories for supervised fine-tuning and the largest open collection of verifiable RL training data for mobile agents, comprising over 2K executable tasks with automatic rewards. (3) Hybrid GUI and app-native tool use: We explore an experimental mobile-use setting where apps expose selected functionalities as app-native tools alongside their GUIs, allowing agents to interleave GUI actions and tool calls within a task. We implement this setting in MobileGym++ with over 300 carefully scoped tools across 50+ apps. Additionally, we introduce MobileGym++ Bench for complex, long-horizon commercial mobile scenarios, supporting both GUI-only and hybrid GUI-tool evaluation on a shared task suite. OpenMobile-2 performs competitively across established benchmarks, including AndroidWorld (79.9) and MobileWorld (50.4), while showing promising transfer to real-device mobile use, nearly doubling SPA-Bench performance from 31.9 to 59.6. All resources are available at https://os-copilot.github.io/OpenMobile2-Home/.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Video-Arena: A Scalable Agentic Video Benchmark for Spatiotemporal Capability
item.description: arXiv:2610.14158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding and tracking a dynamic world are fundamental to visual intelligence. Existing video benchmarks provide limited insight into whether models can maintain a coherent understanding of evolving world state. Building such a benchmark from real-world videos is challenging because the underlying world state is partially observable, making annotations hard to obtain. To close this gap, we introduce Video-Arena, a benchmark that turns competitive games into scalable, verifiable tests of how well models understand evolving world states from videos. Specifically, inspired by how humans understand dynamic events, we evaluate spatiotemporal world state understanding and tracking through three task categories: perceiving critical events, interpreting state updates, and tracking the resulting states. Our pipeline can generate videos and aligned reference labels from game records at scale. To keep evaluation affordable and reproducible, we curate a golden set of 180 tasks across 9 games and run evaluations under two protocols: native visual understanding and tool-assisted agentic analysis. The best-performing systems achieve F1 scores of and under the two protocols, respectively. The result highlights that native models struggle to perceive events reliably, while tool-assisted systems improve event recovery but still struggle to interpret state updates and track the resulting states consistently over time. Our project page is in https://videoarena-bench.github.io
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Disentangling Task-Relevant Latent Dynamics for Reward Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2610.14159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reward design remains a major bottleneck for reinforcement learning in robotic manipulation. Handcrafted dense rewards can compensate for the limited guidance provided by sparse rewards, but require substantial task-specific reward engineering. Learning rewards from videos provides a scalable, data-driven alternative to manual reward design. However, existing video-based rewards are often computed in entangled visual spaces where task-relevant state changes are confounded with extraneous visual variation. As a result, the learned reward may respond to visual distractors instead of actual task execution. To address this limitation, we propose DiTaR (Disentangling Task-Relevant Latent Dynamics for Reward Modeling), a framework for learning dense rewards from heterogeneous videos. DiTaR learns a continuous task-relevant representation from multi-frame video latents through an asymmetric two-stage procedure that suppresses task-irrelevant visual variation. In the task-relevant latent space, we train a history- and language-conditioned rectified-flow model to capture task dynamics and derive a directional dense reward from temporal changes in dynamics compatibility. Together, these components enable reward modeling directly over task-relevant dynamics rather than generic visual variation. DiTaR substantially improves policy learning on MetaWorld-v3 and ManiSkill over video-based reward baselines, and transfers to real-world offline RL through reward relabeling. Reward analyses further show that DiTaR provides more reliable rewards.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Agentic Evolution of SQL Test Generators
item.description: arXiv:2610.14161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated testing has uncovered many logic bugs in Database Management Systems (DBMSs). Existing tools are typically limited to a few SQL dialects and a subset of these dialects' features. Coding agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs) could encode the semantics of additional SQL features into reusable test generators, requiring no additional LLM calls during testing and thus enabling high efficiency and low cost. However, a key challenge is validating the added capabilities in the presence of potential hallucinations. In this paper, we propose Gungnir, an approach for evolving DBMS test generators using coding agents. Our core mechanism is witness replay: the coding agent provides a generation witness recording the database setup and semantic choices needed to generate a target statement. A validator replays these choices through the modified generator and checks that it reproduces the target statement. Historical witnesses serve as regression tests for subsequent modifications. We evaluated Gungnir on SQLite, DuckDB, and PostgreSQL and found 44 bugs confirmed by developers, of which 34 have been fixed. Beyond DBMSs, witness replay could generalize to other systems to guide agents in extending test generators.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Next-Concept Modeling: Fast, Parallel Coarse-to-Fine Text Generation
item.description: arXiv:2610.14162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer parallel sampling for faster generation than autoregressive models, an increasingly important advantage as inference becomes a dominant computational workload. However, DLMs degrade quickly with fewer sampling steps, process the full sequence at every step, and require many passes over the dataset to reach good quality. We introduce Next-Concept Modeling (NCM), a two-stage, coarse-to-fine framework: a multiscale residual VQ-VAE encodes text into a hierarchy of discrete codes, and a transformer generates one level at a time, predicting all codes within a level in parallel. At matched parameter scales, NCM achieves better generative perplexity than the strongest DLM baseline on LM1B while running $21\times$ faster. On OpenWebText, NCM is competitive with the strongest DLM while running $10\times$ faster; on XSum, it matches the strongest DLM's ROUGE-L while being $31\times$ faster. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations. On the reasoning task of Sudoku, NCM outperforms autoregressive and diffusion baselines across all difficulty levels, using fewer function evaluations.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] AutoEnvScaling: Automating the Data Flywheel with Terminal Agents
item.description: arXiv:2610.14163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Terminal agents solve tasks in software engineering and scientific research by executing commands in a terminal. Training them via reinforcement learning (RL) requires diverse and verifiable environments, but these environments are still mostly designed by human researchers, so their supply grows only as fast as researchers can work. We introduce AutoEnvScaling, which treats environment design as a terminal task and uses agents to automate the data flywheel. A proposer agent builds new RL environments from the rollouts of the solver being trained, and the solver's new rollouts guide the next round. By turning environment generation into a terminal task, AutoEnvScaling increases the valid-environment rate by up to 25 times compared to prompt-only generation, at up to 75% lower cost per valid environment. We show that training Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on AutoEnvScaling environments from GPT-5.6-sol improves its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score by 4.3 points over the matched Tmax baseline. The broader goal of AutoEnvScaling is to enable recursive self-improvement (RSI): by making both environment generation and solving terminal tasks, it lets one model co-evolve in both roles. We show that Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, acting in both roles, gains 12.2 points on Terminal-Bench 2.1 and raises its Terminal-Bench 4.0 score from 1.6 to 3.2. The pipeline also generalizes across agentic domains, generating environments for software engineering, computer use, professional work, and GPU kernel programming. Overall, these results show a path toward agents building their own training environments, reducing human reliance and taking a core step toward RSI.
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Do you "see" what I "see"? A Multi-panel Visual Question Answer Dataset for Large Language Model Chart Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.14173v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital libraries increasingly host scientific publications whose figures encode primary research findings, yet making this visual content searchable, accessible, and reusable remains an open challenge. Large language and multimodal models (LLMs/LMMs) provide the possibility to automate many figure parsing tasks such as determining data trends or extracting data from plots. In this work, we consider if these models can reliably support task-oriented visual data analysis when presented with synthetic, but realistic, scientific figures that contain multiple charts. Our Visual Question Answering (VQA) process scaffolds our tasks along a four-level description model from basic conceptual answers to interpretive and analytical understanding. Additionally, we outline our process for synthetically generating our single and multi-panel (charts in which there are multiple panels present) plots and testing the data with various LMMs using quantitative analysis. In general, we find LMMs become less accurate with increasing figure complexity as the number of panels, number of plot elements, and difficulty of questions increase. Finally, because LMM accuracy is expected to change rapidly, our analysis also considers cost relative to performance as a metric to inform future user decisions. We provide the detailed question-answer pairs used in this analysis, along with the code used to generate random plots, question-answer pairs and detailed bounding-box metadata for chart elements. The code and data are available at https://github.com/ReadingTimeMachine/LLM_VQA_MultiPanel and https://huggingface.co/datasets/ReadingTimeMachine/visual\_qa\_multipanel
item.author: cs updates on arXiv.org

item.title: [cs updates on arXiv.org] Unconstrained CTI-REALM with Open-Weights
item.description: arXiv:2610.14180v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Organisations that want language-model agents for security work face a choice between open-weight models, which they can run and audit themselves, and far more expensive closed frontier models. We study that choice on CTI-REALM (arXiv:2603.13517), a benchmark in which an agent turns a threat-intelligence report into a working detection by querying a live telemetry store.
